title: The Neriin in the Pilchard Barrel

setting.location: Trevaskis & Partners Counting House, Wheal Morrow tin-mine, Cornwall
setting.time_period: August 1907, during the annual pilchard festival
setting.environment: A low stone building perched above the cliffs, its single lamp guttering in the storm-wet air, packed ledgers and tin-dust on every surface
setting.description: A violent summer squall has washed out the cliff road to Penzance and sent a rockfall across the mine path, leaving the four surviving partners marooned inside the counting house with the bodies of their colleagues. The nearest farmhouse is four miles across flooded moorland and the tide has swallowed the coastal path. No one may leave until morning light and the storm's end reveal a safe passage — and by then, the poisoner among them has had all night.

solution.motive: Rosalind discovered that her husband Edmund had secretly re-mortgaged her inherited share of the mine to cover his gambling debts, and had forged her signature on a partnership dissolution instrument that would have stripped her of all title upon the festival's close. Killing Edmund before he could lodge the document, and silencing his co-conspirator Jory Nancarrow who witnessed the forgery, was the only way to preserve her inheritance and her independence.
solution.method: Rosalind ground dried neriin — oleander seed — into the saffron powder used to season the traditional pilchard pasties prepared that evening in the counting house kitchen. Edmund Trevaskis and Jory Nancarrow each ate a full pasty; both died of cardiac arrest within two hours. The other partners ate less or none, surviving. Rosalind herself declined the pasties, claiming a stomach complaint.

chain.claim: Both victims died of neriin poisoning confirmed by the post-mortem smell of bitter almonds and the cardiac arrest pattern, ruling out natural causes.

The poison was introduced into the saffron tin used to season the pasties, which was kept in the counting house kitchen — meaning the poisoner had access to that kitchen during the preparation window.

Only persons who remained in the counting house between the storm's onset and the serving of supper had unsupervised access to the kitchen; witnesses establish that only Rosalind Trevaskis was alone in the kitchen during the preparation window.

Rosalind did not eat the pasties she prepared, claiming a stomach ailment she had not mentioned before supper — behaviour inconsistent with innocence and consistent with prior knowledge of the poison.

A forged partnership dissolution instrument bearing Rosalind's signature was found in Edmund's coat pocket, giving Rosalind a concrete financial motive to kill both Edmund and the witness to the forgery, Jory Nancarrow.

solution.how_to_deduce: The post-mortem evidence and the bitter-almond odour on the victims confirm neriin poisoning rather than natural death, establishing that a murder was committed. The contaminated saffron tin in the kitchen shows how the poison reached the food. Witness testimony establishes that Rosalind Trevaskis was the only person left alone in that kitchen during the supper preparation window, giving her unique opportunity. Her conspicuous refusal to eat the very pasties she made, excused by a complaint nobody had heard her mention before, points directly at foreknowledge. Finally, the forged dissolution document found in Edmund's coat — bearing Rosalind's signature but written in Edmund's hand — reveals the financial stake: Edmund had arranged to strip her of the mine, and Jory Nancarrow had witnessed the forgery. With both men dead before the document could be lodged, Rosalind's title was safe. Opportunity, physical evidence, and motive all converge on her alone.

crime.what_happened: Edmund Trevaskis and Jory Nancarrow collapsed within minutes of each other after eating pilchard pasties at the partners' supper. Both men are dead. The cliff road is washed out and the four surviving partners are locked in with the bodies until dawn.
crime.when: Between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. on the night of the pilchard festival, August 1907
crime.initial_discovery: Miner's Captain Cadan Polglase found Edmund slumped over the ledger desk and Jory collapsed near the fire grate; both men were cold to the touch within the hour. The bitter-sweet smell clinging to the bodies drew Polglase's attention.

characters.name: Edmund Trevaskis
characters.occupation: Purser and Senior Adventurer, Wheal Morrow
characters.secret: Edmund had forged Rosalind's signature on a partnership dissolution instrument and secretly re-mortgaged her inherited share to cover ruinous gambling debts in Truro. Jory Nancarrow was the only witness to this forgery.
characters.bio: Edmund Trevaskis is a broad-shouldered, fast-talking man in his mid-fifties who ran Wheal Morrow with the confidence of someone who has never been questioned. He inherited a share from his father-in-law and expanded it through a combination of genuine commercial instinct and ruthless corner-cutting. Those who work for him find him generous in good years and dangerous in lean ones.

characters.name: Jory Nancarrow
characters.occupation: Assayer and Junior Adventurer, Wheal Morrow
characters.secret: Jory witnessed Edmund's forged signature and had been paid a small sum to keep silent. He had recently begun to waver, considering whether to approach Rosalind with what he knew.
characters.bio: Jory Nancarrow is a wiry, precise man of forty who spent twenty years underground before Edmund elevated him to the counting house on the strength of his skill with assay numbers. He is quiet in company, speaks only when certain, and is trusted by the mine's working men in a way that the partners above him never quite are. He keeps a meticulous personal ledger and smells permanently of tin-dust and carbolic.

characters.name: Rosalind Trevaskis
characters.occupation: Minority Adventurer (inherited share), Wheal Morrow; Keeper of the Household Ledger
characters.motive: Rosalind stood to lose her entire inherited share of the mine through a forged dissolution document Edmund planned to lodge with the county registrar at the festival's close. Killing Edmund before lodging, and eliminating Jory as the only witness to the forgery, preserved her title and her independence.
characters.alibi: Rosalind states she was alone in the counting house kitchen from approximately 6:30 p.m. to 7:45 p.m. preparing the festival supper, then joined the others in the main hall. No one corroborates the full preparation period.
characters.secret: Rosalind discovered Edmund's forgery three days before the festival when she found a draft of the dissolution document tucked inside a false-bottomed assay box. She has told no one and has been quietly calculating her options ever since.
characters.bio: Rosalind Trevaskis is a composed, dark-eyed woman of forty-eight who inherited her share of Wheal Morrow from her father, a founding partner. She has endured twenty years of a marriage that moved steadily from indifference to contempt, and she wears that endurance as a kind of armour. Those who underestimate her tend to regret it quietly and at length. She is the one who organises the festival supper each year, and she takes the preparation seriously.

characters.name: Cadan Polglase
characters.occupation: Cap'n and Working Adventurer, Wheal Morrow
characters.motive: Cadan is owed eighteen months of deferred wages Edmund promised but never paid; a ledger entry shows Edmund was about to dissolve the partnership and leave Cadan with nothing. He had argued loudly with Edmund the morning of the festival.
characters.alibi: Cadan was at the mine's engine house with surface-worker Tomas Blewett from 5 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. inspecting the pump gear before the storm hit; Blewett can confirm this. He entered the counting house at 7:40 p.m. and went directly to the main hall.
characters.secret: Cadan has been secretly corresponding with a rival mine consortium in Redruth, considering selling his share of Wheal Morrow's ore data — a betrayal that would constitute breach of partnership and expose him to ruin if discovered.
characters.bio: Cadan Polglase is a stocky, red-faced man of fifty-two who came up through the mine working as a tinner before buying into a small share twenty years ago. He knows the tunnels of Wheal Morrow better than anyone alive and carries the physical marks of that knowledge in his scarred hands and the slight stoop of a man who has spent years in low-ceilinged spaces. He is blunt, occasionally explosive, and almost constitutionally incapable of hiding what he feels.

characters.name: Merryn Pascoe
characters.occupation: Counting House Clerk and Minority Adventurer (purchased share), Wheal Morrow
characters.motive: Merryn Pascoe had loaned Edmund a substantial personal sum two years ago on a handshake, with no written record; Edmund had recently denied the debt entirely and threatened her dismissal if she pressed the matter.
characters.alibi: Merryn was in the counting house main hall from 6 p.m. onwards, tallying the festival's tin receipts in the presence of witness Nancarrow until he fell ill; she never entered the kitchen, which witness Lowena Chegwidden confirms.
characters.secret: Merryn holds a forged receipt she herself created, backdated to substantiate the loan Edmund denied. She has been carrying it for six weeks, terrified it will be discovered and used against her.
characters.bio: Merryn Pascoe is a precise, neatly-dressed woman of thirty-six who bought a sliver of partnership with her late father's savings and has worked the counting house books ever since with a thoroughness that makes her indispensable and unremarkable in equal measure. She has a dry, unhurried way of speaking that people often mistake for coldness; it is in fact a form of vigilance. She has been at Wheal Morrow for twelve years and knows where every number goes.

characters.name: Dreckly Bolitho
characters.occupation: Festival steward and sleeping partner, Wheal Morrow (inherited small share from uncle)
characters.motive: Dreckly's uncle's share was being contested by Edmund on a technicality that would have reverted it to the main partnership; Edmund's death eliminates the claim before it can reach the registrar.
characters.alibi: Dreckly was outside on the cliff path directing the pilchard barrels from 5:30 p.m. until the storm drove him in at approximately 7:50 p.m., witnessed by festival hand Tomas Blewett and at least three pilchard women; he did not pass through the kitchen.
characters.secret: Dreckly has been concealing a chest ailment that is worsening; he fears that if the other partners learn he is ill they will use it as grounds to challenge his capacity to hold his share and force him out at a reduced buy-out price.
characters.bio: Dreckly Bolitho is a lean, weatherbeaten man of forty-four who inherited his small share of the mine along with his uncle's debts and has been fighting to hold both ever since. He has a quick, deflecting sense of humour that he deploys whenever conversation turns serious, which makes him pleasant to drink with and difficult to read. He was not meant to be at the festival this year but arrived two days early, citing a wish to see the pilchard count.

characters.name: Lowena Chegwidden
characters.occupation: Counting House Chare-Woman and Larder-Maid, Wheal Morrow; locally called 'Lowena Close-Hearth' for her habit of keeping near the fire — and near every conversation held beside it
characters.alibi: Present throughout the evening in the main hall and corridor
characters.bio: Lowena Chegwidden is a stout, unhurried woman of sixty who has kept the counting house since Edmund's father's time. She knows every sound the building makes and most of the things that happen inside it. She dislikes drama and has a gift for stating plain facts without embroidery.
characters.statement: I was in the main hall corridor from half-past six onward, carrying the salt-cellar and the bread. Miss Pascoe was at the hall table with the tin tallies the whole time I was passing — never went near the kitchen once. I can swear to that. Mrs Trevaskis was the only one in that kitchen during preparation; I heard her in there alone for over an hour, and when I looked in at a quarter to eight to fetch the bread-cloth she was closing the spice shelf.

characters.name: Tomas Blewett
characters.occupation: Bal-Worker and Festival Hand, Wheal Morrow; nicknamed 'Tomas Grass' by the tributers underground, for a bal-worker who stays at surface is said to work 'on grass' — though Tomas sees more than most men who go below
characters.alibi: Working outside with Cadan and Dreckly until the storm
characters.bio: Tomas Blewett is a young man of twenty-six, broad-shouldered, quietly spoken, hired each festival season for heavy work. He has an accurate memory for times and faces because his father was a Penzance constable who trained him to notice things. He is loyal to whoever pays him fairly and has no stake in the partnership disputes.
characters.statement: Captain Polglase and I were at the engine house from five o'clock — he never left my sight until half-seven when we walked back together and he went straight in the front door. Bolitho was out on the cliff path organising the barrels the whole time too; I passed him three times before the storm came on. Neither of those men went near the house kitchen side at all.

characters.name: Henryk Voss
characters.occupation: Travelling Surgeon-Apothecary from Saxony, storm-stranded at Wheal Morrow during the pilchard festival
characters.alibi: In the mine office with his bag throughout the evening
characters.bio: Henryk Voss is a compact, careful German physician of fifty who was touring the Cornish coast on a working holiday when the storm stranded him at Wheal Morrow. He speaks English with meticulous correctness and carries a worn black bag he is never without. He has no connection to the partnership and no interest in its disputes beyond professional concern for its casualties.
characters.statement: I examined both bodies as soon as I was summoned. The smell on the lips — bitter, almost almond-like — and the cardiac presentation are consistent with oleander glycoside, what we call neriin. It acts within one to three hours of ingestion. Both men ate the saffron pasties at supper; neither the bread nor the cider showed that smell. The pasties are the vehicle — I am as certain as a field examination permits.

evidence.name: Engine House Time-Record
evidence.description: A handwritten pump inspection log kept by Cadan Polglase at the engine house, countersigned by Tomas Blewett, showing continuous entries from 5:00 p.m. to 7:28 p.m. The log's final entry is signed at 7:28 p.m. and the two men's arrival at the counting house front door was noted by Lowena Chegwidden at approximately 7:40 p.m., consistent with the walk time.

evidence.name: Dr. Voss's Field Examination Notes
evidence.description: Written notes made by Dr. Voss within thirty minutes of examining both bodies, describing the bitter-almond odour on the lips, the dilated pupils, and the cardiac arrest presentation. Voss notes these signs are clinically consistent with neriin poisoning from the Nerium oleander plant. His notes specify the pasties as the likely vehicle based on odour comparison with the remaining food items.

evidence.name: Merryn Pascoe's Tally-Sheet Alibi
evidence.description: The festival tin-receipt tally sheets bear Merryn Pascoe's running hand across forty pages of entries, time-stamped by Jory Nancarrow's counter-initials up until 7:55 p.m. — minutes before Nancarrow fell ill. The continuous nature of the entries, consistent in ink shade and pressure, establishes Merryn at the hall table without interruption throughout the preparation window. Lowena Chegwidden's statement corroborates she never left the hall.

evidence.name: Cliff-Path Witness Accounts (Pilchard Women)
evidence.description: Three pilchard-gutting women sheltering in the net store gave statements that Dreckly Bolitho was visible on the cliff path organising barrel stacking from shortly after 5:30 p.m. until the storm drove everyone inside at roughly 7:50 p.m. Their accounts are consistent with Tomas Blewett's statement and with the time Dreckly was seen entering the counting house by Lowena Chegwidden.

evidence.name: Blewett's Verbal Account of Bolitho's Movements
evidence.description: Tomas Blewett's statement places Dreckly Bolitho in continuous view on the cliff path during the supper preparation window; Blewett noted passing him three separate times and exchanging words about the barrel weight each time. Bolitho's entrance through the seaward door — not the kitchen passage — was observed by Blewett himself.

evidence.name: Polglase's Deferred-Wages Ledger Entry
evidence.description: A personal memorandum in Cadan Polglase's handwriting, found tucked in his coat pocket, lists eighteen months of unpaid wages and a marginal note reading 'Edmund to settle by festival close or I take it to the registrar.' The note is dated three days before the festival. It establishes a financial grievance against Edmund but contains no mention of Jory Nancarrow, whose death would bring Polglase no benefit.

evidence.name: Lowena's Testimony of Kitchen Movements
evidence.description: Lowena Chegwidden's statement, given to the group immediately after the deaths, confirms that Rosalind Trevaskis was the sole occupant of the counting house kitchen for the full supper preparation window. Lowena specifies she saw Rosalind closing the spice shelf at approximately 7:45 p.m., placing her hands on the shelf where the saffron tin was stored.

evidence.name: Contaminated Saffron Tin
evidence.description: A small copper tin labelled 'saffron' recovered from the kitchen spice shelf. When Dr. Voss opens it, a faint bitter-almond odour is immediately apparent beneath the spice smell, and a fine dark-brown powder is visible mixed through the saffron — inconsistent with the bright-yellow of pure saffron. The tin was used exclusively for the pasties and was not accessible from outside the kitchen.

evidence.name: Rosalind's Refusal to Eat
evidence.description: Three witnesses — Lowena Chegwidden, Tomas Blewett (who entered at supper-time), and Merryn Pascoe — all independently note that Rosalind Trevaskis did not eat any of the pilchard pasties she herself prepared, claiming a stomach complaint. None of them had heard her mention any ailment earlier in the day. The complaint was raised for the first time at the moment the pasties were served.

evidence.name: Forged Partnership Dissolution Instrument
evidence.description: A formal legal document, partially completed, found folded inside Edmund Trevaskis's inner coat pocket. It purports to dissolve Rosalind Trevaskis's inherited partnership share and bears what appears to be Rosalind's signature — but the signature is written in the same ink and a closely matching hand to Edmund's own marginalia on the document. A comparison of the signature with Rosalind's genuine signature on a festival receipt reveals clear differences in letter formation.

evidence.name: Merryn's Forged Receipt
evidence.description: A creased receipt found in Merryn Pascoe's sewing-bag, written in her own hand but dated two years prior, purporting to record a loan to Edmund Trevaskis. The paper and ink are inconsistent with a two-year-old document — the ink is too fresh and the paper lacks yellowing. It is a forgery, but one Merryn created to substantiate a genuine debt Edmund denied.

investigation_areas.name: Counting House Kitchen
investigation_areas.description: A low-ceilinged stone room behind the main hall, still warm from the range, smelling of saffron, fish-oil and something underneath both — sharper, faintly sweet.
investigation_areas.investigation_prompt: The contaminated saffron tin is on the spice shelf. The kitchen has only one entrance from the main hall. There are no signs of forced entry. A mortar and pestle on the counter carries a faint dark residue distinct from the saffron.
investigation_areas.discovery: On the spice shelf you find a copper saffron tin; inside it a fine dark-brown powder is visibly mixed through the bright saffron, and the tin carries a sharp, bitter-sweet smell quite unlike any spice. On the counter a mortar and pestle bear the same dark residue.
investigation_areas.analysis: Dr. Voss identifies the dark powder as ground oleander seed — neriin. The mortar residue is consistent with the seed being ground here, in this kitchen, within the last several hours.

investigation_areas.name: Main Hall and Partners' Table
investigation_areas.description: The long stone room where the partners dine; the table still holds half-eaten pasties, two toppled cider cups, and the dead men's chairs pushed back at the angles of men who fell.
investigation_areas.investigation_prompt: The tally sheets are on the table and show Merryn's continuous work. Two pasties are untouched on a side plate — the ones intended for Rosalind. A full cup of cider is at Rosalind's place.
investigation_areas.discovery: The festival tin-receipt tally sheets on the table show forty pages of continuous entries in Merryn Pascoe's hand, counter-initialled in a second hand up until the final entry at 7:55 p.m. Rosalind's place setting is notable: her pasty plate is clean but her pasty is untouched on the serving board.
investigation_areas.analysis: Comparison of the counter-initials with Jory Nancarrow's signature on other documents confirms it was Nancarrow countersigning — placing both Merryn and Jory at the main hall table until minutes before Jory collapsed. Rosalind's full, untouched pasty is the only serving returned.

investigation_areas.name: Edmund's Coat and Desk
investigation_areas.description: Edmund Trevaskis's heavy wool coat hangs on the peg behind his desk; the desk itself is spread with ledgers and a brass inkstand, a man's working life interrupted mid-sentence.
investigation_areas.investigation_prompt: The forged dissolution document is in the inner coat pocket. The desk ledger contains entries about the mortgage on Rosalind's share. A locked drawer holds Edmund's personal correspondence.
investigation_areas.discovery: In Edmund Trevaskis's inner coat pocket you find a folded legal document — a partially completed partnership dissolution instrument bearing Rosalind Trevaskis's name as the party whose share is to be reverted, and a signature purporting to be hers.
investigation_areas.analysis: Placing the document beside a genuine receipt signed by Rosalind at the festival office reveals consistent differences in letter formation — the signature on the document is not hers. The ink and hand match Edmund's own marginalia elsewhere on the page.

investigation_areas.name: Engine House and Pump Log
investigation_areas.description: A detached stone building twenty yards from the counting house, smelling of steam-grease and wet granite; the pump log-book sits open on its shelf beside a dripping lamp.
investigation_areas.investigation_prompt: The pump inspection log is here with Cadan Polglase's entries and Tomas Blewett's countersignature, showing continuous presence 5–7:28 p.m. The entries are detailed and technical — clearly not fabricated in advance.
investigation_areas.discovery: The open pump log shows a page of dense technical entries in Cadan Polglase's hand from 5:00 p.m. to 7:28 p.m., each entry countersigned by a second name in different ink.
investigation_areas.analysis: The countersigning hand matches the signature on Tomas Blewett's festival employment paper. The entries describe specific mechanical observations that could only have been made on-site — not written up after the fact.

investigation_areas.name: Cadan Polglase's Coat Pocket
investigation_areas.description: Cadan's working coat hangs on a hook near the mine entrance; it is stained with tin-dust and has the permanent smell of a man who works underground.
investigation_areas.investigation_prompt: The deferred-wages memorandum is here — a genuine grievance document but one that implicates Cadan superficially while being entirely innocent of the actual crime. It will look suspicious but leads nowhere relevant to the poisoning.
investigation_areas.discovery: In Cadan Polglase's coat pocket you find a folded personal memorandum listing eighteen months of unpaid wages owed by Edmund Trevaskis, with a note in the margin reading 'Edmund to settle by festival close or I take it to the registrar,' dated three days prior.
investigation_areas.analysis: Cross-referencing the wages figure with the partnership accounts confirms the debt is genuine and long-standing — but the memorandum names only Edmund, not Jory Nancarrow, whose death brought Cadan no financial benefit whatsoever.

leads.title: The Spice Order Ledger
leads.brief: The counting house housekeeper mentions that the spice supplies were inventoried just before the festival — the record is in the kitchen log.
leads.investigation_prompt: The kitchen purchase log shows saffron and common spices ordered in the normal quantities. There is no entry for any unusual botanical purchase. However, the log shows Rosalind Trevaskis personally collected the spice order from Penzance four days ago — alone, before the storm.

leads.title: The County Registrar's Festival Bundle
leads.brief: A sealed document bundle addressed to the Penzance county registrar was found in Edmund's desk drawer, marked for delivery at the festival's close.
leads.investigation_prompt: The bundle contains a cover letter from Edmund enclosing the dissolution instrument. The letter is dated two days ago. It confirms Edmund intended to lodge the forged document officially — Rosalind's share would have been legally stripped from her within days.

leads.title: Merryn Pascoe's Sewing Bag
leads.brief: Merryn Pascoe was seen tucking something into a sewing bag and looking unsettled when the bodies were found — another partner suggests it is worth examining.
leads.investigation_prompt: The sewing bag contains the forged receipt Merryn created to substantiate her loan claim. It is a red herring — Merryn forged a document but did not poison anyone, and her alibi at the hall table is solid. The receipt is a dead end for the poisoning inquiry.

leads.title: Rosalind's Medical Claim
leads.brief: Rosalind told the group she had a stomach ailment before supper — Dr. Voss is asked whether he was consulted about it earlier in the day.
leads.investigation_prompt: Dr. Voss confirms he spoke briefly with all four surviving partners during the afternoon but Rosalind made no mention of any stomach complaint to him — quite the contrary, she ate heartily from the bread and cheese at midday in his presence. The complaint arose only at the moment the pasties were served.

key_twists: The poison was introduced into a common ingredient rather than a single victim's food, explaining why two men died — players may initially assume a single targeted killing.
Rosalind's forged document motive only becomes visible when Edmund's coat is searched; until then she appears to be a grieving widow with no stake in Jory Nancarrow's death.
Cadan Polglase's wages memorandum makes him look culpable but leads to a firm alibi — the red herring is designed to absorb suspicion from the real culprit early.
Merryn Pascoe's own forgery makes her look guilty of something; players must disentangle her document crime from the poisoning to clear her correctly.

Rosalind's refusal to eat her own food is the most visible single clue, but players must connect it to the saffron tin and the kitchen access testimony before it becomes proof rather than mere suspicion.

_provenance.target_setting: A death at a Cornish tin-mine counting house during the 1907 pilchard festival, with the cliff road washed out and the last four partners trapped inside.

craft_guidance.source: James: "closed circle of suspects"; Rankin: Edinburgh as character; French: location as first decision
Christie (start with method), P.D. James (central mysterious crime), Knox (rule 4: method must be plausible)
Christie: start with murderer and motive, then build outward; worked backward from the solution
James: "each with motive, means and opportunity"; Knox: criminal must appear early
Christie notebooks: alibi construction is explicit planning step

opening_narration: The August gale came in off the Atlantic without warning, and by nine o'clock it had swallowed the cliff road, the mine path, and any hope of reaching Penzance before dawn. Inside the counting house at Wheal Morrow, two men who had sat down to pilchard pasties an hour ago now lay where they had fallen — Edmund Trevaskis face-down across the open ledger, Jory Nancarrow crumpled near the fire grate, a faint bitter-sweetness still hanging in the warm air above them. Cap'n Cadan Polglase was the first to find them, and the first to understand that the storm outside was the least of the evening's troubles. Four people remain in this room: four partners in the mine, four people who shared that supper, four people who cannot leave until the tide retreats and the moorland drains enough to walk. Morning is a long way off, and the night has only just begun.

violations.message: E4 exonerates ['Dreckly Bolitho'] but no witness, lead or area reveals it
